title: Chapter 172 – Seven and One
html:
[The Seventh Door – Lin Jian]

Kito takes his time.

That is the first surprise. Jian had expected the young man to throw himself at the door, to burn bright and fast, in the manner of those who have waited four hundred years and cannot stand another minute. Instead he takes his hands off the black surface, and wipes them on his tunic as though they were damp, and says, in the tone of a host at the end of a long dinner, "Give me an hour. There are a few things I'd like to say, and I'd like to say them properly."

"We have nine days," says Duan Ke, roughly.

"We have nine days and an hour." The silver eyes crinkle. "The hour is for me. It's a very small thing to ask."

Nobody argues. Jian leans against the cold wall and watches the young man move down the line of children, as a man might walk down a shore at the end of a long holiday, touching each thing once before it is gone.

He stops at Hai Ren first. The monk bows, and the seer bows back, deeper. "You are the Settling," says Kito. "I saw you once, in a dream. You were very tired."

"I am often tired."

"I know. It suits you." He lifts a silver hand. "Will you do something for me?"

"If I can."

"When the door opens, there will be pain. I'd like to not feel it." The corner of his mouth lifts. "It's a petty vanity. I've been brave for four hundred years and I'm out of practice."

Hai Ren inclines his head. "I will hold the stillness."

"Thank you." Kito's smile softens. "That's all I wanted."

* * *

The joke takes up most of the hour.

It is Bell who asks. She does it in the middle of a pause, in her blunt healer's way, standing with her arms folded and her chin up. "What was it? The joke. The one Mei told you."

Kito turns. His eyes light.

"Ah. You've heard." He sits down on the bench with a flourish and pats the wood beside him. "Come. Sit. All of you. I will tell it exactly as she told it, and you must promise not to laugh until the end."

They sit. The children press close, Ao in Jian's lap, Tao on the floor with his chin on his knees, Mo Yan cross-legged at the seer's feet with her charcoal. Yue and Bell on the bench, Duan Ke and Cheng Hui and Hai Ren and Zhen Li in a half circle. The black door breathes at their backs.

"There was a chicken," says Kito, "who lived near a lighthouse."

Tao snorts. Kito holds up a warning finger.

"Every night the chicken looked up at the great light, going round and round, and thought: what a splendid egg. And every morning the lighthouse keeper came out with a bucket of feed, and the chicken said: Excuse me. Is that your egg?"

"And what did the keeper say?" Ao whispers.

"He said: No. That is the sun."

A pause.

"And the chicken said: Well. It's very bright. Is it laying?"

The silence stretches. Ao looks at Jian. Jian looks at Bell. Bell has her lips pressed together with the expression of a woman who has been told not to laugh and is considering whether to obey.

Then Tao, from the floor, says with enormous scorn, "That doesn't make sense."

"No," says Kito happily. "That's the point. She was nine. She told it with a completely straight face. And when I laughed, she looked at me and said, Why are you laughing? It's not a joke. It's a chicken."

Duan Ke makes a noise like a stifled sneeze. Cheng Hui's shoulders are shaking. Even Hai Ren has put a hand over his mouth. And then Mo Yan, cross-legged at the seer's feet, begins to hiccup, silently, with her whole thin body, and the cracked silver bell goes ringing through Jian's skull, and the whole corridor erupts.

They laugh until they cry. It goes on for a long time. Ao falls off Jian's lap. Zhen Li, who has forgotten his own name, laughs so hard that his lantern flares. And Kito, in the middle of them, with his head thrown back and his silver face wet, says in a choked voice, "You see? You see? It's the best joke in the world."

"It's terrible," says Tao, wiping his eyes.

"It's perfect," says Kito.

* * *

He gives them each something.

It is not much. A word, a touch, a fragment of the future that he turns over in his fingers like a coin. To Cheng Hui he says: You will write the first true history of the Nine, and it will be wrong in only three places. To Duan Ke: You will break your sword again, and it will be worth the breaking. To Hai Ren: You will learn that stillness has a sound. To Zhen Li, who is looking at him with his blank bright eyes: You will remember your name. Not today. But soon, and from an unexpected quarter.

"What does that mean?" Zhen Li asks.

"I haven't the faintest idea," says Kito. "I only see the shape."

To Tao he says nothing. He only ruffles the small boy's hair with one silver hand, and Tao, to his own astonishment, does not pull away.

To Ao he says: Count the cracks. One of them is a duck.

And to Mo Yan he says, very quietly, so that only she and Jian can hear: You will speak. One day. Not soon. Not for a long time. But you will, and the first thing you say will be a thing you have been saving for years. He lowers his voice further. Don't waste it.

The girl looks up at him with enormous dark eyes. She nods.

Yue is last. He kneels in front of her, so that their faces are level, and says nothing at all for a moment. Then he reaches out and, very gently, lays one finger on the small dent at her breastbone, where the pebble sits.

"It's still there," he says.

She mouths: Yes.

"It's holding on. It's holding on for you." The silver eyes are warm. "I'd tell it to rest, if I thought it would listen. But I think it's rather like you. It doesn't."

Yue's eyes fill. She takes his hand in both of hers and holds it, and Kito lets her.

* * *

When it is Jian's turn, the young man doesn't speak at all.

He just stands. The two of them face each other in the lamplight, the old man with his staff and the boy with no staff, and for a long time neither moves. Behind Kito the great door breathes, a slow patient swell, and the white seam flickers.

"I'm sorry," Jian says at last.

"For what?"

"For the shed. For the lamps. For—" He stops. His voice is shaking. "For all of it. For taking a nineteen-year-old and a girl of eleven and a hundred and fifty thousand strangers and asking them to carry what I could not."

"You didn't ask." Kito's smile is gentle. "That's the thing. You never asked. We offered. It's a very different thing."

"I wish it had not been necessary."

"So do I." A rueful laugh. "I wish a lot of things. I wish I'd learned to cook. I wish I'd seen the sea. I wish I'd told my mother I loved her before I left." His eyes meet Jian's. "But I'm glad it's me, Lin Jian. Do you understand? Out of all of them, all the Nine, all the Operators, all the people who might have stood here. I'm glad it's me."

"Why?"

"Because I'm the one who knew." He says it simply. "I saw the whole of it, when I was nine. Every part. The tree, the Door, the girl, the tide. And I thought, I can't bear it. And then I thought, someone has to. And then I thought, why not me?" The bright face softens. "It's not courage. It's only that when you know how it ends, there isn't anything left to be afraid of."

Jian closes his eyes. The tears run down his face and he does not wipe them.

"Tell your mother thank you," says Kito. "For the soil."

"I will."

"And tell Mei—"

"The joke was not that bad."

"Exactly." The young man grins. "She'll know what it means."

* * *

Bell catches him alone in the last minutes of the hour.

She takes his sleeve, and draws him a few steps down the corridor, away from the children, and when she speaks it is in a whisper that shakes with fury. "You will not let him."

"Bell—"

"You will not. I do not care if he is a seer. I do not care that he has been dead four hundred years. He is nineteen years old, and he is going to die in front of seven children, and you are going to stand there and allow it."

"I tried to stop him."

"Try harder."

"I did." His voice is low. "I said no. He did not listen. He is the holder. It is his door." He puts a hand over hers. "Bell. He is not being brave for us. He is being brave for the tree. He told me. He has spent four hundred years knowing what he would do, and he is at peace with it."

"That is not the same as it being right."

"No." He swallows. "It is not."

She stares at him. Her eyes are bright and furious and wet.

"I hate this," she says. "I hate every single part of it. Every time I think we are done with the sacrifices, there is another one."

"I know."

"And I hate that you are not arguing."

He gives her a small, tired smile. "I think I have used all my arguments."

She drops his sleeve. She draws a long breath, and wipes her face with the heel of her hand, and when she looks at him again the fury has become something quieter and much harder to bear.

"Then we will make it count," she says. "Every day. Every one of them. We will make sure he was not wrong."

"Yes."

"And you will not die for it."

"I will try not to."

"You will do better than try." She straightens. "Go. Say your goodbyes."

* * *

The fold begins when the hour is done.

Kito goes to the door. He lays both hands flat on the black surface and stands there with his head bowed, a thin silver figure against the immense darkness. The white seam blazes. The breathing on the other side quickens, and swells, and the stone floor under Jian's feet begins to hum.

Gather, says Kito. His voice is quiet. Close. Hold hands. All of you.

They form a ring. Ao, Tao, Mo Yan, Zhen Li, Hai Ren, Duan Ke, Cheng Hui, Jian. Yue and Bell stand in the center, with their arms round the smallest. Eight Operators and two others, in a close hot circle at the foot of the great black door.

Don't let go, Kito says. Whatever you see. Whatever you hear. It's a long road, and it folds. If you let go, you'll be left in the fold, and I can't fetch you.

"We will not," says Jian.

Good. The silver outline brightens. Hai Ren?

"I am ready."

Then count to three.

"One," says Ao, in a small clear voice.

"Two," says Tao.

"Three," says the whole ring together.

The door opens.

* * *

It does not swing. It does not slide. It simply is no longer closed. The black surface folds back on itself like a page turning, and where it was there is nothing, a gap in the world, a hole in the dark, and the white light that pours out is so bright that Jian cannot look at it.

The heat hits him like a wall.

He feels the ring tighten. He feels Ao's hand in his, and Duan Ke's on the other side, and the shuddering of the whole circle as it leans into the light. There is a roaring that is not sound. There is a sense of falling, upward, sideways, through a place with no floor. He opens his mouth and cannot hear his own scream.

And through it all, steady as a heartbeat, he can feel Kito.

The seer is not in the door. He is the door. His outline has stretched across the whole of the gap, a silver web of lines thinner than hair, and the lines are fraying. They snap one by one. Each snap rings like a string on a harp, and each is a small pure note, and each is followed by the faint soft sigh of a man who has put down something heavy.

Oh, says Kito, from very far away. It's like being poured out. I didn't know. It's like water.

Kito—

It doesn't hurt. The voice is distant, amused. Hai Ren's doing. Thank him. A pause. Isn't that odd? I'm not afraid at all.

The roar swells. The world turns inside out. Jian squeezes his eyes shut and hangs on to the small hands in his, one after another, until the whole ring is a single trembling animal made of eleven pairs of fingers.

Tell her, whispers Kito. Tell Mei. Tell her it wasn't that bad.

It was perfect, says Jian, and weeps.

The last string snaps.

Silence.

* * *

No sound. No light. No weight. For the space of a long breath there is nothing in the world but the pressure of eleven small hands, and a stillness so complete that Jian thinks he has died. Then the floor comes up to meet his feet, as gently as a hand under a sleeper's head, and the dark begins to be dark again.

They are standing on stone.

It is cool. It is dry. It is utterly still. The ring of hands has loosened, and they stand blinking in the dark, gasping, unharmed, exactly as they were in the corridor. The only difference is the air. It is thicker here. It smells of earth and root and growing things, and under that, so faint that he almost mistakes it for his own imagination, of apples.

Jian opens his eyes.

The first thing he sees is that the door is gone. The corridor is gone. In their place is a floor of pale polished stone, and beyond it, a darkness so vast that his mind recoils from the measure of it.

Then Zhen Li lifts his lantern.

The light spreads. It spills out across the floor, golden and soft, and where it falls the dark retreats, and Jian sees that he is standing at the edge of a plain.

It is a plain of beds.

They stretch away in every direction, in rows so long and so straight that they seem to meet at the horizon. Row on row on row. Beds of pale wood and pale linen, each with its small brass number, each with its sleeper, each breathing in the slow, deep, regular rhythm of the very deeply at rest. There is no wall to the hall. There is no roof. There is only a vault of living roots, enormous and black and silver-leafed, arching overhead like the ribs of a world, and from every root hangs a thousand soft pale lights.

Nobody speaks.

"Nine million," whispers Cheng Hui. His voice cracks. "Nine million, four hundred thousand."

"Are they all asleep?" asks Ao.

"Yes."

"Is anyone awake?"

"No, little one." Jian puts a hand on the small shaggy head. His own voice is thick. "Not one. They have been waiting a very long time."

Behind them, where the door had been, there is nothing at all but a smooth wall of root, and a small flat stone set into the earth, engraved with a single character: seven.

Beneath it, someone has scratched, in a fine neat hand, a tiny drawing of a duck.

* * *

Before the stair, there are the nine beds.

Jian sees them as the others are lighting the lamps for the climb. He has wandered a few paces from the group, leaning on his staff, drawn by a gleam of brass at the edge of the light. They stand a little apart from the long rows, in a half circle at the foot of the stair, as though set aside for company: nine beds of pale wood, nine pillows, nine folded blankets. Each has a small brass plate.

Eight are empty. The sheets are turned down. The pillows are plump. The beds have the look of being kept, as a room is kept for a guest who may arrive at any hour.

He reads the plates.

MA RUO-LIN.

BRENN.

THE CARTOGRAPHER.

THE FERRYMAN.

THE VEILED.

SHEN OF THE THIRD HALL.

KITO.

He stops at the seventh. The plate is bright, newly polished, and someone, long ago, has scratched at the bottom, in a fine neat hand, a tiny duck.

The eighth bed's plate is blank.

And the ninth, the last bed in the half circle, has a plate that reads, in letters worn almost smooth by a thousand touches, ETHAN COLE. The sheets on it are rumpled, as though a man had just got up. On the pillow lies a single folded paper.

Jian stands very still. He does not touch it.

Brother, says the boy, in his small round room. They kept a bed for him.

Yes.

Even though he left.

Even so. Jian's throat tightens. Perhaps they knew he would come back.

He turns away from the beds. At the foot of the stair, Bell is waiting, with a lantern in one hand and the other held out. He takes it, and they begin to climb.

* * *

Cheng Hui and Duan Ke argue about the war at the foot of the stair.

They do it in low voices, while the children sleep in a heap on the bottom steps, and Hai Ren sits motionless against the wall with a cloth pressed to his nose. Jian listens from a few steps down, leaning on the rail, and does not interrupt.

"Four thousand," says Duan Ke. "It said four thousand two hundred. On the Wall, with what, three hundred men?"

"With the stone, and the pit, and the arrow-slits. I have read the old Wall plan." Cheng Hui's voice is calm. "The Wall was designed to hold ten times its number, for about a day. After that, it depends on the wall."

"The wall can't hold."

"No. It cannot." The scholar turns a page. "But a wall is not the only thing that holds. A line holds. A will holds. I have read about a thousand fights in which the defenders were outnumbered and lost, and a hundred in which they won. The difference was never the numbers."

"What was it?"

"Whether somebody stayed." Cheng Hui closes the book. "The ones who won were always the ones in which somebody did not leave."

Duan Ke is silent for a time. Then he says, gruffly, "I'm not leaving."

"I know."

"I'll be at the front."

"I know that as well." A pause. "I will be behind you, writing it all down. It is what I do."

The sword boy gives a short, unsteady laugh. He wipes his eyes with his sleeve. "You're an odd sort of friend," he says.

"I have been told." The scholar's smile is faint. "But I notice, my dear Duan Ke, that you have not told me to go."

* * *

They climb for a day and a night.

There is a stair, of course. The Nine thought of everything. It spirals up through the roots at the edge of the plain, narrow and steep, carved into the living wood of the tree. Duan Ke goes first, with the pale blade drawn. Hai Ren follows. The children are carried in turn, Ao on Bell's hip, Tao on Duan Ke's back, Mo Yan on Cheng Hui's shoulders, with her charcoal stub clutched in his hair. Jian climbs on his own legs. He does not ask for help.

It nearly kills him.

By the sixth hour his breath is a rattle. By the ninth he has coughed twice into his sleeve and tucked the cloth away before anyone can see. Bell sees. She says nothing, but at the next landing she pushes a black wax pill between his teeth and holds his jaw shut until he swallows.

"Thank you," he says hoarsely.

"Do not thank me. Walk."

He walks.

The stair climbs on. The air changes. It grows warmer, and thinner, and the smell of apples grows stronger, until it is almost a taste. The roots overhead thin to branches. The pale lights fade, and a faint real gray light begins to show above, the gray of a dawn.

* * *

At the twelfth hour, the boy speaks.

Brother.

I am here.

I've been thinking about the joke. His voice is small and warm. It doesn't make any sense. The chicken. The lighthouse. I keep going through it.

Neither did I.

But I laughed.

We all did.

Why? The boy is quiet a moment. Why does a thing that doesn't make sense make everyone laugh so hard?

Jian climbs three steps before answering. His breath scrapes. The pale rope-rail is smooth under his hand, worn by a thousand years of other hands. I think, he says slowly, that sometimes people need to be reminded that there are things in the world with no reason in them at all. Things that are only there because they are. A chicken. A lighthouse. A girl of nine, telling a joke with a straight face.

Because it's not a joke. It's a chicken.

Yes.

That's the best thing anyone's ever said.

It is. Jian smiles, though his eyes sting. I think it might be the whole of the universe, in nine words.

The boy is quiet for a long while. Then, in a very small voice: I'm going to miss him.

So am I.

Will we remember?

Always. Jian touches the wall of the stair. I will tell it to everyone. Starting with Mama. And you will keep the stone.

The ninth one?

Yes. He closes his fingers on the rail. The color of a duck's egg, I think.

The boy laughs, wetly. And the stair climbs on.

* * *

At the sixteenth hour, the whole world shakes.

It is a single huge convulsion. It rolls up from below, from the plain of beds, from the earth itself, and the stair bucks like a boat in a gale. Jian is flung against the wall. Ao screams. Someone drops a lantern, and the light skitters and goes out, and in the dark he hears the groan of the great roots, a long deep wooden cry, like a ship's hull under strain.


He reads it with his heart pounding, in the dark, with the stair still shuddering round him. Then, in the dimness, a hand finds his. It is Bell's. She is white to the lips.

"Jian," she says. "Is that—"

"Yes."

"How long?"

"A day and a half." He swallows. "Perhaps less."

Ao has stopped crying. He is clinging to Bell's neck with the rabbit crushed between them and his small face set in an expression of fierce, silent attention, as though he were counting something. Perhaps he is. Perhaps they all are.

Above them, through the shaking roots, a thin gray light is growing at the top of the stair. And with it, faint and far and unmistakable, comes a sound that he has not heard in a hundred years: the long, high, cracked bellow of the Wall's horn.

The tide has begun.
